newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major, boosted by poll, appeals for voter trust.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major, boosted by poll, appeals for voter trust.

text.p: An opinion poll showing a dramatic plunge in the opposition Labour party's lead on Wednesday electrified the campaign for Britain's May 1 election, turning what had looked a certainty into an open race.

Conservative Prime Minister John Major, scenting the chance of an extraordinary victory, resumed his attack on opposition leader Tony Blair, appealing to voters to trust his six years of experience in office and not the novelty of Blair.

"I appeal to you: don't let whatever doubts you may have had about the Conservative Party in the past weigh with you when the future of the United Kingdom may be at stake," he told a rally in Aberdeen, Scotland.

The ICM poll in The Guardian newspaper slashed Labour's lead from 14 to just five points, the first time the opposition's advantage has fallen to single figures since November 1993. Its lead has been as high as 28 points in the past six weeks.
Blair, odds on favourite for almost two years to win the election, appealed to supporters to step up their efforts and not fall prey to complacency.
Asked whether Major would win, Blair told supporters in a London suburb: "Let's hope not.
"Get rid of this Conservative government and get a Labour government in its place. We can only do it if you are going to come out and support us on May 1," he said at a campaign rally.
Major is convinced his personal popularity is his deeply divided party's best hope of winning an unprecedented fifth straight term in office.
The ICM poll showed 33 percent of voters backed Major as the best prime minister, compared with Blair on 32. The gap was 13 points in Blair's favour on April 2.
Conservative strategists said the poll showed Major's tactic of focusing on Europe was working despite splits in his own party over policy on a single European currency.

Labour economics spokesman Gordon Brown pointed to a Gallup poll in Wednesday's Daily Telegraph putting Labour 21 points ahead, an increase of five in a week, saying: "There's so many polls, you have to take them with a pinch of salt."
ICM defended its methods on Wednesday as other polling organisations urged caution, suggesting the result could prove to be a "rogue" and Labour's support could bounce back.
But bookmakers William Hill said they had cut the odds on the Conservatives winning the May 1 election to 7-2 from 9-2.
In opposition since 1979, Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing to win power on May 1. Major won a 21-seat majority in 1992.
